guides.title: The Nebula Class
guides.summary: The Nebula class is a 24th-century Federation starship class — a multi-role cruiser sharing components with the Galaxy class and distinguished by its interchangeable mission pod. Ships of the class include the Sutherland, the Phoenix and the T'Kumbra.

sections.heading: Design and Lineage
sections.body:
The Nebula class is a Federation starship class of the mid-twenty-fourth century, developed in the same design generation as the Galaxy class and sharing much of its component family: saucer geometry, warp nacelles and major systems are common to both lines. Where the Galaxy class spreads its volume across an extended engineering hull, the Nebula compresses the same essentials into a shorter, denser spaceframe, with the secondary hull tucked directly beneath the saucer and the nacelles mounted close inboard.

The result is a smaller, more economical ship that keeps most of the larger class's capability. Federation yards — Utopia Planitia among them — produced Nebulas in substantial numbers precisely because the class reused proven components: construction was faster, spares were interchangeable across two fleets of ships, and crews cross-trained easily between the classes. In fleet registries the Nebula is variously described as a cruiser, an explorer and a multi-role platform; the ambiguity is honest, because the class was built to be reassigned. Its defining feature, the interchangeable mission pod, makes the same hull a different ship from one refit to the next.

sections.heading: The Mission Pod
sections.body:
The Nebula's signature is the superstructure pod carried on a dorsal pylon above and behind the saucer. The pod is a swappable module, fitted out for the ship's current assignment and exchangeable at a starbase in the course of a refit. Documented configurations include long-range sensor arrays for survey and early-warning work, tactical modules carrying additional weapons and defensive systems, and mixed scientific fits built around a specific programme; fleet records also describe triangular sensor platforms and cargo variants, and some hulls have flown with no pod at all.

The pod is what makes the class's flexibility real rather than nominal. A Nebula assigned to deep survey and the same Nebula recalled to a border squadron are materially different vessels, without a new keel being laid. Starfleet's force planners came to rely on that property: in peacetime the pods leaned scientific, and in the emergencies of the 2360s and 2370s tactical modules moved out of storage in numbers. Engineering literature credits the Nebula programme with proving modularity at cruiser scale, a lesson visible in several later Starfleet classes.

sections.heading: Capabilities and Layout
sections.body:
Beneath the pod, the Nebula is recognisably a sibling of the Galaxy class. Its saucer carries the bulk of crew quarters and laboratories; the underslung engineering section houses the warp core and main deflector; and its interior standard — from bridge modules to sickbays — is drawn from the same catalogue as its larger contemporary. Crew complements in fleet records run in the several hundreds, varying with the fitted pod and mission, and the class supports the full range of standard Starfleet operations: extended independent cruises, planetary survey, transport and escort, and combat when required.

In action the class gave a good account of itself. A Nebula's armament is close to a Galaxy's, in a smaller and somewhat handier hull, and wartime task forces used the class in the line of battle rather than behind it. Its limits are those of its economies — less internal volume, less endurance between resupply, fewer of everything a longer hull carries spares of — and captains' assessments preserved in the record describe the trade plainly: nearly the capability at a fraction of the ship, provided the mission fits the pod.

sections.heading: Service History
sections.body:
Nebulas entered service in the 2360s and were quickly everywhere the fleet was. The class turns up across the operational record of the era: border patrol and blockade during the Klingon and Cardassian crises, deep survey and stellar cartography programmes, convoy escort, and the major fleet actions of the Dominion War, where Nebulas fought at the front alongside the Galaxy-class ships they resembled. The class also paid the price of ubiquity — Nebula hulls are recorded among the losses at Wolf 359 and in the war's fleet engagements.

The record preserves individual moments as well as statistics. The USS Phoenix, under Captain Benjamin Maxwell, demonstrated the class's fighting power in the gravest way, conducting unauthorised attacks on Cardassian targets in 2367 that Starfleet itself had to end. The USS Sutherland, with Lieutenant Commander Data in temporary command, held a picket line in the blockade mounted during the Klingon civil war. Ships of the class continued in service well into the century's later decades, refitted and re-podded as doctrine changed — which was precisely the career the design had promised.

sections.heading: Notable Ships of the Class
sections.body:
Fleet registries list Nebula-class ships in numbers, and several names recur in the historical record. The Phoenix and the Sutherland carry the class's most-taught episodes, described above. The T'Kumbra, under Captain Solok, was notable as a vessel crewed entirely by Vulcans — a reminder that Starfleet's ships are sometimes cultural statements as well as instruments. Other hulls of the class appear throughout the logs of the 2360s and 2370s — among them the Farragut, the Merrimac, the Monitor, the Leeds, the Bellerophon and the Prometheus of the Bajoran-sector science missions — in roles from ferrying flag officers to holding sections of a battle line. Records differ on the fates of some; the class's loss lists from Wolf 359 and the Dominion War have gaps that historians still argue over.

Taken together the roster illustrates what the Nebula class was for. No single famous ship defines it the way a flagship defines its class; the Nebula's monument is distribution. For three decades, when Starfleet needed a capable ship somewhere quickly, the ship that arrived was, more often than not, a Nebula with the right pod.

guides.title: The Oberth Class
guides.summary: The Oberth class is a small Federation science vessel class — survey and research ships such as the USS Grissom, USS Tsiolkovsky and USS Pegasus — in continuous service from the 23rd century into the 24th.

sections.heading: Role and Design
sections.body:
The Oberth class is a small Federation starship class built for science: survey, research, environmental monitoring and the patient cataloguing work that fills most of Starfleet's log entries and few of its histories. The class entered service in the twenty-third century and remained in production and operation for an extraordinary span thereafter, making it one of the longest-serving spaceframe designs in Starfleet's inventory.

An Oberth is modest by every fleet measure. Crews recorded for the class run from a few dozen up to around eighty, armament is light, and speed and endurance are those of a laboratory rather than a cruiser. Those economies are the design's point. The class was cheap to build and to run, simple enough for scientific institutions and reserve crews to operate, and numerous enough that Starfleet could afford to station one wherever a question needed watching — over a newly seeded planet, beside an unstable star, along a quiet border. Fleet culture summarises the class with rough affection: the Oberth is the ship Starfleet sends when it wants to know something rather than do something.

sections.heading: An Unusual Configuration
sections.body:
The Oberth's silhouette is distinctive: a compact saucer-form primary hull carried on twin pylons that also bear the warp nacelles, with a separate lower hull — a smooth, sensor-dense pod — suspended beneath, connected only through the pylon structure. Fleet engineering literature discusses the arrangement more than any other feature of the class, because the lower hull's isolation appears deliberate: separated from the crewed spaces, it is an ideal mounting for sensitive instruments, hazardous samples and experiments best kept at arm's length.

Records differ on the interior details, and the class's technical documentation has fed a long-running argument among historians of naval architecture about how the lower hull was accessed and what, on any given hull, it contained — configurations plainly varied across the class's long production run and many refits. What is not disputed is the design's fitness for its work: the geometry gave the Oberth clean fields of view for its sensor suites, generous isolated volume for its laboratories, and a hull that could be reconfigured for a new programme without touching the crewed decks. For a science vessel, those were the measures that mattered.

sections.heading: A Long Service Life
sections.body:
Oberths were already in Starfleet service in the 2280s and were still being encountered on active duty a century later — a longevity almost unique among Federation classes. The explanation is partly economics and partly fitness: the class was inexpensive to maintain, its scientific role aged more slowly than tactical roles do, and successive refits kept its instruments current even as its spaceframe design passed out of fashion. Starfleet operated Oberths alongside ships three generations younger, and civilian and academic institutions within the Federation flew the class as well.

The long life had a sombre side. Small, lightly armed and often thinly crewed, Oberths appear in the loss registers of the twenty-fourth century with regularity — destroyed in the Borg incursion at Wolf 359, lost to hazards their instruments were studying, or overwhelmed in encounters a cruiser would have survived. The fleet's assessment was unsentimental about the arithmetic: the class's affordability was inseparable from its fragility, and the missions it flew were valuable precisely because they placed a ship where nothing was supposed to happen. Usually nothing did; the registers record the exceptions.

sections.heading: Ships of the Record
sections.body:
Several Oberths carry stories larger than their tonnage. The USS Grissom conducted the Genesis Planet survey of 2285 and was destroyed at that mission by Klingon attack, with the loss of nearly all aboard — the class's starkest demonstration of what light armament means. The USS Tsiolkovsky was lost in 2364 while monitoring a collapsing star, after a contaminant incapacitated her crew; the investigation aboard her hulk nearly claimed the Enterprise as well. The USS Pegasus became the class's most consequential ship for the worst reason: her secret equipment trials in 2358 violated the Treaty of Algeron, killed most of her crew, and surfaced twelve years later as one of Starfleet's gravest internal scandals when the cover-up unravelled.

Against these stand the quieter entries: the Yosemite, battered but recovered during a plasma-streamer study; the survey hulls of the Bajoran and border sectors; and dozens of ships whose logs record nothing but data delivered. The class's historians point out, accurately, that the famous Oberths are famous because something interrupted the science.

sections.heading: Assessment and Legacy
sections.body:
The Oberth class is remembered as the definitive statement of a Starfleet conviction: that a fleet built for knowledge needs small, honest instruments as much as great explorers. The class institutionalised the idea of the dedicated science vessel — a ship whose entire design budget is spent on what it can measure — and later classes in that role, whatever their improvements, are working in a template the Oberth set.

Its name honours a foundational theorist of spaceflight from Earth's early rocketry era, and the class wore the association well: unglamorous, essential, ahead of what its resources should have allowed. Officers who served aboard Oberths describe the experience in consistent terms — too small, too slow, too close to the phenomena, and the best scientific posting of a career. When the fleet's memorial rolls are read, the class is disproportionately present for its size, and when the Federation's star charts are consulted, an unremarked share of every sector's data traces to some Oberth that spent a year in orbit of something no one else would visit. The class's monument, its historians conclude, is the accuracy of the map.

guides.title: The Ambassador Class
guides.summary: The Ambassador class was a Starfleet heavy cruiser of the early twenty-fourth century, the bridge between the Excelsior and Galaxy generations of starship and starships; its most famous vessel, the USS Enterprise-C, was lost defending the Klingon outpost at Narendra III.

sections.heading: Role and Place in the Fleet
sections.body:
The Ambassador class entered Starfleet service in the early decades of the twenty-fourth century as the Federation's principal heavy cruiser, filling the long interval between the venerable Excelsior class and the Galaxy class that followed a generation later. It was conceived as a true multi-role starship: large enough to lead a border squadron or carry a diplomatic mission, versatile enough for deep-space exploration, and durable enough to stand in the line of battle when required.

In its years as the fleet's front-line cruiser the class carried Federation colours through a period of cold tension with the Romulan Star Empire and an uneasy, still-forming peace with the Klingon Empire. Ships of the class were regularly assigned to patrol contested borders, escort convoys, and host negotiations, precisely because a single hull could do all three without returning to a starbase to be refitted. By the 2360s newer designs had taken over the leading role, but Ambassador-class vessels remained in active service throughout that decade and into the Dominion War era, a measure of how sound the original design proved to be.

sections.heading: Design and Capabilities
sections.body:
In profile the Ambassador class reads as a transitional form, and deliberately so. The broad elliptical primary hull, integrated engineering section and paired warp nacelles anticipate the flowing lines of the later Galaxy class, while the overall arrangement still honours the cruiser layout Starfleet had trusted since the Constitution era. The class was substantially larger than the Excelsior that preceded it, with a crew complement in the several hundreds and internal volume generous enough for large science departments, diplomatic quarters and extensive shuttle facilities.

Armament centred on phaser emitters and photon torpedo launchers arranged for all-around coverage, backed by deflector shields that were, for their day, among the strongest in the fleet. Records credit the class with respectable cruise and maximum warp figures for its generation, though exact performance varied between early and late production hulls; later ships incorporated refinements to the nacelles and deflector geometry that are visible in surviving registry imagery. The design's real strength was balance rather than any single superlative, and that balance is why the class aged so gracefully in service.

sections.heading: The Enterprise-C and Narendra III
sections.body:
The most celebrated ship of the class was the USS Enterprise, NCC-1701-C, fourth Federation starship to bear the name. In 2344, under the command of Captain Rachel Garrett, the Enterprise-C answered a distress call from the Klingon outpost at Narendra III, which had come under attack by four Romulan warbirds. Hopelessly outmatched, the Enterprise-C engaged the attackers anyway and was destroyed with nearly all hands.

The sacrifice was not wasted. Klingon accounts of a Federation crew dying in defence of Klingon lives carried enormous weight in the Empire, and historians credit the action at Narendra III with cementing the Federation-Klingon peace that held through the following decades. Starfleet temporal records add a stranger footnote: an incident in 2366 in which the Enterprise-C was displaced twenty-two years forward through a temporal rift, briefly producing an altered history in which the Federation stood at open war with the Klingon Empire. The ship's return to its own time, and to its fate, restored the timeline. Accounts of survivors taken prisoner after the battle differ, and portions of the record remain sealed.

sections.heading: Notable Ships of the Class
sections.body:
Beyond the Enterprise-C, registry records list a number of Ambassador-class vessels with notable service histories. The USS Horatio, commanded by Captain Walker Keel, was destroyed in 2364 under circumstances later tied to an attempted infiltration of Starfleet Command by parasitic lifeforms. The USS Adelphi conducted the ill-fated contact mission at Ghorusda, whose casualties prompted lasting revisions to first-contact protocols. The USS Yamaguchi stood in the line at Wolf 359 in 2367 and was lost with most of that fleet against the Borg.

The USS Zhukov served as a science and transport vessel through the 2360s, frequently exchanging personnel with the Enterprise-D. The USS Excalibur took part in the fleet blockade during the Klingon civil war of 2368, operating under a temporary command staff drawn from the Enterprise-D as part of the tachyon detection grid that exposed Romulan resupply of the Duras forces. Individually these are ordinary service records; taken together they show a class trusted with every kind of assignment the fleet had to give, from quiet survey work to the worst days in Starfleet history.

sections.heading: Service Legacy
sections.body:
By the standards Starfleet applies to capital designs, the Ambassador class must be judged a success. It held the fleet's centre for a generation, absorbed refits gracefully, and retired slowly rather than abruptly, with hulls still performing secondary duties during the Dominion War. Its deeper legacy is architectural: design elements pioneered on the Ambassador — the enlarged elliptical saucer, the integrated engineering hull, the treatment of habitability and diplomatic capacity as military virtues — flowed directly into the Galaxy and Nebula classes that defined the fleet of the 2360s and 2370s.

Officers who served aboard Ambassador-class ships in their prime went on to senior commands across the fleet, and the class remains a fixture of Academy design curricula as the worked example of a transitional generation done well. Above all, the name Narendra III keeps the class in memory. A starship class is finally judged by what its crews did with it, and by that measure the Ambassador class stands with the most honoured designs in Starfleet history, remembered less for its specifications than for a single act of sacrifice.

guides.title: The Nova Class
guides.summary: The Nova class was a small Starfleet science vessel of the late twenty-fourth century, a ship built for short-range planetary surveys and research; among ships and starships of its size it is remembered chiefly for the USS Equinox, stranded in the Delta Quadrant.

sections.heading: Purpose and Profile
sections.body:
The Nova class entered service in the 2370s as Starfleet's dedicated light science vessel, the replacement in role for the ageing Oberth class. Where explorers such as the Galaxy and Intrepid classes were built to go far, the Nova was built to look closely: its design brief called for short-duration planetary research, system surveys and analysis missions conducted within reach of Federation support. The class is small by fleet standards, with a crew complement of roughly eighty and a hull optimised for sensor performance rather than speed or endurance.

Its maximum sustainable velocity of approximately warp eight placed it among the slower front-line designs of its generation — an accepted limitation, since a Nova was never intended to cross great distances alone. Internal volume is devoted overwhelmingly to laboratories, sensor pallets and sample-handling facilities. In fleet planning terms, the Nova was the instrument a sector command dispatched when a phenomenon needed weeks of patient measurement rather than a passing scan from a larger ship's long-range array, and in that narrow role it had no equal for its cost.

sections.heading: Design Features
sections.body:
The Nova class compresses the standard Starfleet configuration into a compact, close-coupled form: a flattened arrowhead primary hull blended into a short engineering section, with warp nacelles carried low on down-swept pylons and the main deflector set into the forward face of the secondary hull. The silhouette is unglamorous and entirely functional. Sensor pallets occupy an unusually large fraction of the exterior surface, and the class's planetary sensor suite was considered exceptional for a hull of its size.

A distinctive feature is the Waverider, an auxiliary atmospheric craft docked flush into the underside of the saucer, giving survey teams a purpose-built vehicle for sustained work inside a planet's atmosphere where transporters or standard shuttles would be poorly suited. Armament is modest — phaser arrays and a small number of torpedo launchers sufficient for self-defence — and the shield grid is rated for hazard protection more than for battle. Crew accommodation is spare but complete, and the class was certified for independent operation lasting months at a time, provided the ship remained within reasonable range of resupply and repair.

sections.heading: The USS Equinox
sections.body:
The class's most infamous ship was the USS Equinox, commanded by Captain Rudolph Ransom. In 2371 the Equinox was seized by the entity known as the Caretaker and dragged some seventy thousand light-years into the Delta Quadrant — the same displacement suffered by the USS Voyager. For a Nova-class vessel the situation was close to hopeless: a ship rated for planetary surveys, with a top speed near warp eight, faced a journey home projected in decades through a region for which it carried neither the defences nor the endurance.

Heavily damaged and starved of resources, the surviving crew crossed a line Starfleet holds absolute. They discovered that captured nucleogenic lifeforms could be converted into a fuel that dramatically enhanced their warp drive, and they continued the killings knowingly. When Voyager encountered the Equinox in 2376 the truth emerged; the Equinox was destroyed in the confrontation that followed, and its handful of survivors were taken aboard Voyager stripped of rank. The Equinox file is now taught at the Academy as an ethics case: the record of a crew that chose getting home over what home stands for.

sections.heading: Variants and Later Service
sections.body:
The Nova class was designed with an unusually long upgrade horizon for a small ship, and fleet records show the spaceframe absorbing successive improvements to sensors, computer cores and defensive systems through the late 2370s. One curious entry comes from Starfleet's temporal archive: sensor logs recorded during an incident aboard the USS Voyager preserve the image of the USS Rhode Island, a heavily refitted Nova-class variant operating in the early twenty-fifth century of a possible future, with revised nacelles and substantially upgraded systems. Temporal records of futures that may never occur are treated with caution, but the archive is at least evidence of what Starfleet's own designers believed the hull could grow into.

In the fleet of record, Nova-class ships served through the Dominion War in survey, patrol and support roles, where their sensor suites made them useful pickets despite their modest speed. The class continued in production after the war as Starfleet rebuilt its science arm, and postwar assignments returned it to the work it was drawn for: patient, unglamorous, indispensable surveys of the worlds the Federation had been too busy to study.

sections.heading: Legacy
sections.body:
The Nova class is easy to overlook and hard to replace. It carries no famous battles, and its best missions ended with a data archive rather than a commendation — which is precisely the point of the design. Fleet science depends on hulls cheap enough to build in numbers and capable enough to be trusted alone with a phenomenon for a season, and the Nova filled that need better than any predecessor.

Its reputation carries one permanent shadow: the Equinox, whose name has become shorthand for what isolation and desperation can do to a Starfleet crew. Historians are careful to separate the ship from the failure — nothing in the class's design caused what happened in the Delta Quadrant, and the same displacement was endured by another crew without the same choices. Taken whole, the record shows a modest ship that did modest work reliably, charted more worlds than most explorers twice its size, and earned its place in the fleet's long middle rank: the vessels that quietly perform most of the Federation's actual science while the great explorers take the histories.

guides.title: The Prometheus Class
guides.summary: The Prometheus class was Starfleet's advanced tactical starship of 2374, a warship among ships and starships able to split into three warp-capable sections in multi-vector assault mode; its prototype was hijacked by Romulans and recovered by two holographic doctors.

sections.heading: A Ship Built for Combat
sections.body:
The Prometheus class broke with a century of Starfleet convention: it was designed, openly and from the keel, as a warship. Authorised during the deteriorating security situation of the early 2370s and launched as a prototype in 2374, at the height of the Dominion War, the class was intended for deep-space tactical assignments — the missions where a lone Federation ship might have to fight its way in and out without support. The design brief prized speed, automation and firepower over the laboratories and diplomatic facilities that define most Starfleet hulls.

The prototype was among the fastest vessels in the fleet at launch, with a rated maximum in excess of warp 9.9, and its automation was so extensive that a skeleton crew — in an emergency, a mere handful of officers — could fight the ship. Nothing about the Prometheus was apologetic. It was the clearest statement Starfleet had yet made that exploration survives only when the fleet can also win wars, and the class remains the reference example of Federation warship design of its era.

sections.heading: Multi-Vector Assault Mode
sections.body:
The class's signature capability is multi-vector assault mode. On command, the ship separates along two structural seams into three independent sections — the saucer and two segments of the engineering hull — each with its own warp propulsion, shielding and armament. The three sections then fight as a coordinated squadron under computer synchronisation, executing attack geometries no single hull can manage: simultaneous runs from different bearings, envelopment of a larger opponent, or a dispersal that forces an attacker to divide fire among three fast targets.

Separation and re-docking can be performed under way, and the automation is thorough enough that the sections can fight effectively with almost no one aboard. The mode was proven in earnest on the prototype's very first flight: it disabled a pursuing Federation Nebula-class starship while the ship was in hostile hands, and later, with control recovered, held its own against Romulan warbirds. Tactical assessments since have been consistent — multi-vector assault multiplies a single hull into a squadron, at the price of a complexity that only heavy automation makes survivable in practice.

sections.heading: The Prototype Hijacking of 2374
sections.body:
The prototype's shakedown became one of the stranger incidents in fleet records. In 2374 agents of the Romulan Tal Shiar seized the Prometheus in Federation space, killed her skeleton crew, and set course for Romulan territory with the most advanced ship in Starfleet as their prize. Retaking her fell to an unlikely boarding party of two: the prototype's own Emergency Medical Hologram, a Mark II, and the Mark I EMH of the USS Voyager, transmitted across tens of thousands of light-years through an alien relay network from the Delta Quadrant in what was, at the time, the only means Voyager had of reaching home.

The two holograms — immune to the measures the hijackers could bring against living boarders, and able to move anywhere in the emitter-equipped ship — incapacitated the Romulan prize crew and then fought the vessel, clumsily by their own admission, until Starfleet forces arrived. The incident secured the prototype's return, carried the first proof to Starfleet Command that Voyager's crew had survived, and entered Academy lore as the engagement won by two doctors.

sections.heading: Systems and Defences
sections.body:
Beyond the assault mode, the Prometheus carried the most advanced defensive fit of its generation. Regenerative shielding could recover strength under sustained fire, and the spaceframe was engineered so that each separated section remained a balanced warship in miniature, with its own phaser coverage, torpedo capacity and deflector protection. The class was also the first in Starfleet equipped with holographic emitters on every deck, freeing the Emergency Medical Hologram from sickbay to reach casualties anywhere aboard — or, as the 2374 hijacking demonstrated, to act for the crew when no crew remained.

Automation ran deeper than in any previous design: damage control, section coordination and much of flight operations could proceed with minimal supervision, reflecting a wartime assumption that trained officers would be the scarcest resource aboard. The cost of all this was complexity. Maintenance demands were heavy, the automation required constant certification, and fleet engineers of the period debated openly whether so sophisticated a design would age well in ordinary service. As a statement of what Federation technology could achieve in 2374, however, it had no rival anywhere in the fleet.

sections.heading: Service and Legacy
sections.body:
The class entered limited production after the prototype's recovery, in numbers befitting a specialised tactical design rather than a general-purpose cruiser. Prometheus-class vessels appear in fleet movements through the closing years of the Dominion War and afterward; one stood in the formation that escorted the USS Voyager home on its return to the Alpha Quadrant in 2378.

The design's longer legacy is easier to trace in ideas than in hull counts. Its deck-wide holographic emitters normalised the notion of holograms as working crew rather than sickbay fixtures. Its automation studies fed directly into later fleet doctrine on minimal crewing and computer-directed damage control. Multi-vector assault itself remained rare — records differ on how widely the capability was repeated in later classes, and some analysts hold that the mode solved a wartime problem the postwar fleet no longer faced. The Prometheus is remembered accordingly: not as the pattern for everything that followed, but as the moment Starfleet demonstrated, under the pressure of war, exactly how far it could push a starship when it chose to.

guides.title: The Jem'Hadar Attack Ship
guides.summary: The Jem'Hadar attack ship was the Dominion's standard small warship — a fast, expendable fighter among the ships and warships of the Dominion War, whose phased polaron beams cut through Federation shields in the first years of contact.

sections.heading: The Dominion's Standard Warship
sections.body:
The Jem'Hadar attack ship was the most numerous vessel of the Dominion military and the first Dominion hull the Alpha Quadrant powers learned to fear. A compact, beetle-shaped craft — Starfleet crews took to calling it the bug ship — it covered the roles a dozen Federation classes divide among themselves: fighter, patrol ship, raider, escort and assault transport. Encounter records begin in 2370, when the Dominion announced itself with a series of attacks on ships and colonies operating through the Bajoran wormhole in the Gamma Quadrant.

The design is Dominion doctrine made solid. The ship is fast at impulse and at warp, agile, heavily armed for its displacement, mass-produced in Dominion yards, and treated — exactly like the Jem'Hadar soldiers aboard — as expendable. Attack ships rarely fought alone, operating instead in wings of two or three that could press a larger vessel from multiple bearings at once. Throughout the Dominion War they formed the numerical backbone of every Dominion fleet, screening the heavy battlecruisers and absorbing losses at a rate no Alpha Quadrant power could have sustained.

sections.heading: Weapons, Shields and the Odyssey Lesson
sections.body:
The attack ship's principal armament is the phased polaron beam, and in the first years of contact it made the class disproportionately lethal. Federation shield grids of 2370 offered almost no resistance to polaron fire; beams passed through as though the shields were not raised at all. The lesson was administered brutally in the class's first major engagement. When the Galaxy-class USS Odyssey entered the Gamma Quadrant in 2370 in response to the Dominion's seizure of Deep Space Nine personnel, three attack ships cut her defences apart — and as the Odyssey withdrew, one deliberately rammed her, destroying the ship with all hands.

The ramming was unnecessary by any tactical measure, and Starfleet analysts have always read it as it was intended: a message about what the Dominion was willing to spend. Starfleet and the Klingon Defence Force eventually developed shield modulations that restored meaningful protection against polaron weapons, closing the worst of the gap by the war's outbreak in 2373. Even then, the attack ship remained dangerous in numbers, and numbers were the one thing the Dominion never lacked.

sections.heading: A Ship Without Comforts
sections.body:
Boarding parties who captured attack ships found interiors unlike anything in Alpha Quadrant service. There is no viewscreen; the commanding Vorta and the Jem'Hadar first pilot the ship through virtual sensor headsets that feed imagery directly to the wearer. There are no chairs at most stations, no crew quarters worth the name, no food stores or replicators — Jem'Hadar soldiers take no nourishment but ketracel-white, dispensed by their Vorta overseer — and no dedicated medical facilities, because the Dominion does not treat wounded Jem'Hadar so much as replace them.

Every cubic metre saved is spent instead on engines, weapons and troop capacity. Starfleet engineers who studied captured hulls described them as instruments rather than vessels: a ship built by a power that regards its crews as ammunition. The absence of comforts is not austerity for its own sake; it is an exact statement of how the Founders value the beings who serve them, and officers who flew captured examples reported that the ship itself made that point more eloquently than any intelligence briefing ever managed.

sections.heading: Captured Hulls in Starfleet Service
sections.body:
Starfleet operated captured attack ships on several occasions, and the intelligence yield was considerable. In 2373 personnel from Deep Space Nine recovered a downed but largely intact attack ship in the Gamma Quadrant and held it against determined Jem'Hadar counterattack at heavy cost in lives; the hull was returned to Federation space and became the fleet's primary reference on polaron weaponry, Dominion sensor design and the ketracel-white distribution system.

In 2374, early in the Dominion War, a captured attack ship — records suggest the same hull — carried a Starfleet crew under Captain Benjamin Sisko deep into Cardassian space on a mission that destroyed the Dominion's principal ketracel-white storage facility in the Alpha Quadrant, a blow that strained Jem'Hadar supply lines for months afterward. Crews who flew captured examples confirmed what the interiors implied: the ship handles superbly, sees well and shoots well, and gives its occupants nothing else whatsoever. Several Alpha Quadrant intelligence services sought captured hulls of their own, and the study of these ships shaped anti-Dominion tactics for the remainder of the war.

sections.heading: Assessment
sections.body:
Fleet assessments of the attack ship return to the same conclusion: the design cannot be judged apart from the power that built it. Once polaron countermeasures matured, a single attack ship was a manageable opponent for a prepared Starfleet cruiser — its shielding was comparatively light and its endurance short. But the Dominion never intended the class to fight even. It was built to arrive in numbers, to be spent without hesitation, and to be replaced from production lines that Alpha Quadrant intelligence never once saw slow, even at the height of the war.

The willingness of Jem'Hadar crews to ram — demonstrated against the Odyssey in the first encounter and repeated throughout the war — meant no engagement against attack ships was safely won until every hull was destroyed. Starfleet's after-action doctrine absorbed the lesson permanently: engage attack ships at range, never assume a crippled one is finished, and never mistake the smallness of the ship for the smallness of the threat. As a pure instrument of war, analysts rank it among the most efficient designs on record.

guides.title: The Akira Class
guides.summary: The Akira-class heavy cruiser, Starfleet's torpedo-heavy twin-hulled warship of the 2370s. Covers the class's catamaran design, its weapons pod, and the service of these starships against the Borg at Sector 001 and through the Dominion War.

sections.heading: A Twin-Hulled Heavy Cruiser
sections.body:
The Akira class breaks with the classic Starfleet arrangement of saucer, neck, and secondary hull. Its primary hull is a thick, broad saucer that carries most of the ship's volume. From the saucer's aft quarters, two parallel hulls sweep back like the arms of a catamaran, each ending in a warp nacelle, and a pair of dorsal pylons arch up and over to suspend a heavy weapons pod above the centerline. The effect is a ship that reads as a single braced structure rather than a hull with appendages, and the bracing is the point: the frame is engineered to hold together under fire and hard maneuvering rather than to maximize internal volume.

The class is markedly larger than the escorts of its generation but smaller than the great exploratory cruisers, with a crew in the several hundreds. Records describe an unusually generous through-deck hangar arrangement running through the saucer, with bow and stern doors, giving the class a shuttle and auxiliary craft capacity out of proportion to its size, though registries differ on how many hulls carry the full fit.

sections.heading: Built for a Darker Decade
sections.body:
The Akira belongs to the generation of Starfleet designs laid down after the Borg incursion of 2366 and 2367, when a single cube destroyed thirty-nine starships at Wolf 359 and reached Earth orbit. That battle ended a long period in which Starfleet had treated dedicated combat capability as a secondary concern, and the classes that followed, among them the Defiant, Steamrunner, Saber, and Norway, were shaped by the lesson.

The Akira was the heavy end of that response: a cruiser intended to stand in a battle line, escort task forces, and deliver massed torpedo fire, while remaining a true multi-role starship able to carry out patrol, transport, and relief work between crises. Its designers accepted shorter unsupported range and plainer accommodations than an exploratory cruiser would carry, and spent the savings on structure, redundancy, and armament. The class entered service in the early 2370s, in time for the conflicts it had been built to expect, and production continued through the Dominion War years at multiple yards.

sections.heading: Armament and Defenses
sections.body:
The class's signature weapon is its torpedo battery. The dorsal pod is in effect a dedicated torpedo platform, with multiple launchers firing forward and aft, and further tubes are set into the hull; registries credit the class with more launch tubes than any comparable Starfleet cruiser of its day, though the exact count varies by refit. The arrangement lets an Akira put sustained, overlapping torpedo salvos onto a target while keeping its own axis of approach flexible. Phaser arrays laid along the saucer's dorsal and ventral surfaces provide all-around beam coverage for close work and point defense.

Defensively the ship relies on heavy shield generators, a deeply braced spaceframe, and system redundancy: critical functions are duplicated across the saucer and the catamaran hulls so that damage to one region does not silence the ship. The through-deck hangar adds a further layer of flexibility, allowing the class to operate large numbers of auxiliary craft for search and rescue, boarding support, or fighter operations without depending on external facilities.

sections.heading: Service Record
sections.body:
Akira-class ships were prominent in the defense of Sector 001 in 2373, when the Borg drove a second cube toward Earth. The USS Thunderchild is recorded among the ships that engaged the cube in Earth orbit as part of the fleet that finally destroyed it.

In the Dominion War the class served throughout the front: in the fleet actions around Deep Space 9, in Operation Return, in the invasion of the Chin'toka system, and in the final battle for Cardassia. Task force commanders used Akiras as the sturdy middle of mixed formations, heavier and steadier than the escorts, more expendable than the capital ships, and as strike leaders for torpedo runs against Dominion battle lines. Losses were real, but the class absorbed the war better than most, and its hulls came out of the conflict with reputations for bringing damaged formations home. After the war Akiras remained front-line ships, appearing in fleet deployments well into the closing years of the century.

sections.heading: Place in the Fleet
sections.body:
The Akira marks the point where Starfleet stopped pretending its cruisers were not warships. Earlier generations folded tactical capacity into hulls whose declared purpose was exploration; the Akira's architecture states its purpose in silhouette. Yet the class never became a pure combatant. Its hangar capacity made it a natural platform for disaster relief and evacuation, its sensor fit supported ordinary survey work, and in peacetime deployments Akiras carried out the same patrol, escort, and diplomatic-transport duties as any cruiser.

That balance is why the design endured after the emergency that produced it had passed. Fleet planners found that a ship built to survive a battle line was also a ship that survived everything else: ion storms, first-contact standoffs, long patrols far from repair yards. The class settled into the role the Miranda had held a century earlier, as the dependable, numerous, unglamorous middle of the fleet, expected to be wherever it was needed and to still be there when the emergency ended.

guides.title: The Borg Cube
guides.summary: The Borg cube, the Collective's vast cubic vessel and the most feared class of starship on record. Covers the cubes' decentralized design, drone complements, adaptive defenses, the battles of Wolf 359 and Sector 001, and known variants and weaknesses.

sections.heading: Geometry as Doctrine
sections.body:
A Borg cube is exactly what its name states: a vessel built as a cube, without bow, stern, or any concession to direction. The shape is the Collective's engineering philosophy made visible. A cube has no forward weapons array because every face is a weapons array; no bridge to target, no engine block to cripple, no vulnerable neck or nacelle. Its surface is not plated but latticed, an exposed grid of conduits, structural members, and machinery extending inward, so that the distinction between the ship's skin and its interior is largely meaningless.

Observed cubes measure on the order of three kilometers along an edge, though records differ between encounters and the Collective evidently builds to more than one scale; mass estimates run to the hundreds of millions of tonnes. Nothing about the design is intended to intimidate, which is precisely why it does. The cube communicates that its builders regard aesthetics, aerodynamics, and the conventions of naval architecture as irrelevant, and that they have been correct so far.

sections.heading: A Ship Without a Bridge
sections.body:
No one commands a cube from a chair. Its functions are distributed across the entire structure: propulsion, weapons, sensors, and processing are replicated in thousands of redundant nodes, coordinated by the linked minds of the drone complement rather than by a central computer in any conventional sense. Boarding parties report corridors without signage, chambers without doors, and no spaces resembling quarters, galleys, or recreation. Drones do not live aboard a cube so much as function within it, regenerating in alcoves set directly into the machinery.

Complement estimates vary widely; captured data and survivor accounts place tens of thousands of drones aboard a typical cube, and considerably more on the largest. Each cube carries a central plexus linking it to the Collective across interstellar distances, and subspace transceiver arrays maintain that connection continuously. The consequence of this architecture is a ship that treats damage as bookkeeping. Whole sections can be vaporized without loss of capability, and cubes have been observed continuing an engagement while visibly gutted, because nothing essential lived in the sections that burned.

sections.heading: Assimilation and Adaptation
sections.body:
A cube's weapons serve its purpose, and its purpose is acquisition. Engagement records describe high-energy tractor beams that seize vessels many times smaller and hold them while a cutting beam sections the hull for study or salvage; directed energy weapons and torpedoes handle whatever resists, and shield-draining fields strip a target's defenses in moments.

The cube's defining capability, though, is adaptation. Its shields and weapons adjust to attack in real time: an energy weapon that damages a cube in its first firing may accomplish nothing by its third, as the Collective analyzes the frequency and modulation and compensates. Crews facing the Borg learned to rotate firing frequencies, to strike with projectiles and improvised methods, and to expect any successful tactic to be a single-use tactic. Damage the cube does absorb, it repairs with disquieting speed, drones rebuilding structure even while the engagement continues. Assimilation extends inward as well: boarded technology and captured personnel are incorporated, and each encounter leaves the Collective knowing more about its opponent than the opponent has learned about the cube.

sections.heading: Engagements in Federation Space
sections.body:
Starfleet's first recorded engagement with a cube came in 2365, in System J-25, when a single vessel demonstrated that the Federation's finest explorer could neither outfight nor outrun it. Two years later a cube entered Federation space directly. At Wolf 359 in 2367 it destroyed thirty-nine of the forty starships assembled against it, with the loss of some eleven thousand lives, and proceeded to Earth orbit unescorted. It was stopped not by weapons but through the Collective's own link, when access gained through a captured and recovered officer allowed a regeneration command to be induced, destroying the cube.

In 2373 a second cube reached Earth, and a massed fleet destroyed it in orbit after concentrated fire was directed against a critical point, though records note the cube released a sphere before its destruction. Later encounters, chiefly in the Delta Quadrant, fill in the picture of cubes operating in formation, in numbers, and across the Collective's transwarp network, against which the Federation's two victories read as narrow and unrepeatable.

sections.heading: Variants and Vulnerabilities
sections.body:
The standard cube is not the only form. Tactical cubes, sheathed in additional hull armor over the exposed lattice, have been observed where the Collective expects sustained resistance. Spheres serve as auxiliaries and scouts, and cubes have been recorded carrying spheres internally.

Whatever the variant, the known vulnerabilities are few and mostly structural to the Collective itself. A cube ignores intruders and small craft until they register as threats, a calculated indifference that has been exploited more than once. Its dependence on the Collective link means that commands inserted through that link, as at Earth in 2367, can accomplish what fleets cannot. Power distribution junctions and the central plexus offer points of attack for those able to reach them. And the Collective's adaptation, its greatest strength, lags novelty: wholly unfamiliar weapons or tactics succeed exactly once. None of this amounts to a reliable countermeasure, and Starfleet's standing assessment is blunt. Engagements with a cube are won, when they are won, by means the cube has not seen before and will never permit again.

guides.title: The Cardassian Galor Class
guides.summary: The Galor class, mainline warship of the Cardassian Union: the ochre-hulled cruisers that enforced the occupation of Bajor and fought the Dominion War. Covers the starships' spiral-wave disruptors, wing tactics, the Keldon-class derivative, and the fleet's fate.

sections.heading: Profile and Construction
sections.body:
The Galor class is the mainline warship of the Cardassian Union, and for most of the late twenty-fourth century it was the shape Cardassian power took when it crossed a border. The hull is flat and elongated, widening aft into swept flanks and rising at the bow into a raised head section, the whole finished in the ochre and umber tones characteristic of Cardassian shipbuilding. The silhouette is often compared to weapons and tools from Cardassia's own iconography, and the resemblance is generally taken to be deliberate.

Construction is robust but austere. Cardassian yards built the class in large numbers under the Central Command's direction, and the design accepts plainer accommodations, tighter compartments, and less redundancy than a Federation counterpart in exchange for economy and speed of production. Crew complements run to several hundred. Boarding reports describe interiors organized around hierarchy and surveillance, with duty stations sighted from command positions and records systems threaded through every compartment: a ship, in other words, that reflects the state that built it.

sections.heading: Armament and Tactical Character
sections.body:
The Galor's principal weapons are spiral-wave disruptors, mounted along the hull and concentrated in the bow, where the raised head section carries the ship's heaviest emitter. The forward armament is the point of the design: Cardassian doctrine favors the committed attack run, and a Galor delivers its best fire along its axis of approach. Aft and flank coverage is thinner, a known weakness that Cardassian commanders offset through maneuver and formation discipline rather than refit. Torpedo armament and shielding are serviceable but unremarkable by the standards of the great powers.

Ship for ship, a Galor of the 2360s was assessed as no match for a Federation heavy cruiser, and Central Command knew it; the class was never meant to fight alone. Galors operate in pairs and attack wings, sequencing their runs to keep a target's defenses turning, and in numbers they are dangerous to anything afloat. Against lighter opposition, Bajoran raiders, Maquis fighters, or civilian shipping, a single Galor was overwhelming, which was, for most of its service life, the actual job.

sections.heading: Doctrine and Deployments
sections.body:
The class is inseparable from the Cardassian Union's occupations and border wars. Galors enforced the occupation of Bajor, escorting labor convoys and ore carriers and holding position over a subject world. Through the 2350s and 2360s they fought the long border conflict with the Federation, and after the treaty that ended it they patrolled the Demilitarized Zone, where the Maquis insurgency made every convoy escort a potential ambush. Central Command used the class as its all-purpose instrument: patrol cruiser, transport escort, orbital enforcer, and diplomatic presence, the same hull serving each role with the same blunt vocabulary.

The Obsidian Order, the Union's intelligence service, was formally forbidden warships of its own, a prohibition whose limits became apparent in 2371, when a covert fleet including Keldon-class derivatives was revealed in the Orias system and then annihilated by the Jem'Hadar in the Omarion Nebula. That disaster, and the humiliations of the Klingon invasion of 2372, left the Galor fleets weakened and the Union looking for a patron.

sections.heading: The Dominion Years
sections.body:
Cardassia found its patron in 2373, when the Union joined the Dominion and Galor wings began flying alongside Jem'Hadar attack ships. Dominion engineering upgraded the class where it counted, in weapons yields, shielding, and coordination systems, and the war that followed put Galors into every major action: the assault on Deep Space 9, the defense against Operation Return, the battles for the Chin'toka system, and the long attritional fighting along the front.

The alliance was never a partnership. Cardassian crews watched the Dominion spend their ships as screening forces and their worlds as staging grounds, and the resentment that accumulated broke open in the war's final hours. At the Battle of Cardassia in 2375 the Cardassian fleet turned on the Dominion mid-engagement, Galors firing on the ships they had escorted in, a reversal that helped end the war and that the Dominion answered with the devastation of Cardassia Prime. The class fought its last major battle, in effect, on both sides.

sections.heading: Derivatives and Aftermath
sections.body:
The Galor's principal derivative is the Keldon class, an enlarged development with additional engine and weapons sections built onto the same basic hull, giving greater firepower and endurance at the cost of the original's economy. Keldons served openly with the military and, notoriously, in the Obsidian Order's secret fleet. Records also describe progressive refit standards within the Galor type itself, and Starfleet intelligence assessments distinguish several configurations, though Cardassian records of the distinctions did not all survive the war.

After 2375 the surviving Galors became the core of a much-reduced fleet, serving a shattered Union through reconstruction under the postwar settlements. Their continued presence was double-edged: the same silhouette that had enforced the occupation of Bajor now patrolled relief corridors into Cardassian space. Assessments from the period differ on numbers, but agree on the essential point. The class that had carried Cardassian ambition outward for forty years ended the century carrying what remained of Cardassia home.

guides.title: The Excelsior Class
guides.summary: The Excelsior class began as the failed transwarp Great Experiment of the 2280s and became the longest-serving workhorse in Starfleet history — the class of Sulu's Excelsior and the Enterprise-B, still fighting on the front lines a century after its launch.

sections.heading: The Great Experiment
sections.body:
The Excelsior class began as a gamble. Laid down in the early 2280s at the San Francisco Fleet Yards, the prototype NX-2000 Excelsior was built around an experimental transwarp drive and promoted through the fleet as the Great Experiment — the ship that would make the standard warp scale obsolete and every existing cruiser second-rate. She was the largest, most automated, most confident vessel Starfleet had yet built, and her first commander was given to boasting about her before she had properly flown.

The gamble failed publicly. During the crisis surrounding the theft of the USS Enterprise in 2285, Excelsior was ordered to pursue and could not: her engine control systems had been quietly sabotaged by the Enterprise's own chief engineer, and the pride of the fleet drifted to a halt in spacedock's shadow. The transwarp program itself never recovered — the drive missed its promised performance in trials, and by the end of the decade the project had been wound up and the hull refitted with conventional, if excellent, warp engines.

sections.heading: From Failure to Workhorse
sections.body:
What survived the transwarp program's cancellation was the spaceframe, and the spaceframe was superb. Recommissioned NCC-2000 with standard drive, Excelsior proved fast, roomy, long-legged, and straightforward to build, and Starfleet ordered the class into series production. The design settled into every role the fleet possessed: explorer, patrol cruiser, convoy escort, task force flagship, testbed for refits. Where the exotic drive had failed, the ordinary virtues — range, capacity, maintainability — succeeded on a scale no one had projected.

The numbers tell the story better than any single ship. Excelsior-class hulls remained in production, in one variant or another, for decades, and in front-line service for the better part of a century; fleet records of the 2360s and 2370s still show them everywhere, from deep survey to the desperate defensive battles against the Borg and the Dominion. Very few designs in Starfleet history have served across so wide a span, and none of the others began life as a public embarrassment.

sections.heading: Design and Layout
sections.body:
The class follows the classic Starfleet arrangement — saucer primary hull, cylindrical engineering hull, twin nacelles on swept pylons — enlarged and refined. At around 460 metres with a complement in the several hundreds, an Excelsior offered far more internal volume than the Constitution class it succeeded, and the design spent that volume on endurance: larger fuel and cargo capacity, extensive laboratories, and engineering spaces sized for major maintenance on long deployments far from home.

The original transwarp lineage left permanent marks. The engineering hull is long for the ship's beam, laid out around what was to have been the experimental drive train, and the class's power distribution proved unusually accommodating of upgrades — one reason refits kept the design competitive for so long. A prominent variant adds a distinctive extension to the engineering hull and revised nacelle pylons; the USS Enterprise-B was completed to this standard. Handling is remembered fondly in service memoirs: for a ship of her size, an Excelsior turns and accelerates like something considerably smaller.

sections.heading: Excelsior Under Sulu and the Enterprise-B
sections.body:
The class's rehabilitation is inseparable from Captain Hikaru Sulu, who took command of Excelsior herself around 2290 and spent three years on a cataloguing survey of gaseous planetary anomalies in the Beta Quadrant — exactly the unglamorous, methodical work the class was built for. In 2293 Sulu ended that mission by taking his ship uninvited into the Khitomer crisis, standing with the Enterprise against conspirators trying to destroy the Federation-Klingon peace. The Great Experiment's hull, under a captain who believed in it, helped save the alliance the next century was built on.

That same year the USS Enterprise NCC-1701-B, an Excelsior-class ship of the revised variant, was launched from Earth. Her maiden voyage — a press event flown with unfinished systems — met a distress call, and in the rescue of El-Aurian refugees from a mysterious energy ribbon the ship lost a section of her secondary hull and, so the record stood for decades, James T. Kirk himself. The class thus carries both bookends of an era: Sulu's vindication and the Enterprise line's costliest launch.

sections.heading: A Century of Service
sections.body:
The Excelsior class outlived its origins so thoroughly that later generations mostly forgot them. Through the first half of the 24th century the class formed the backbone of the fleet's cruiser strength, and hulls such as the Hood, the Repulse, and the Crazy Horse appear continuously in deployment records of the 2360s. The class paid the price of ubiquity in the era's disasters — Excelsior-class ships were among the losses at Wolf 359 — and refitted hulls fought on through the Klingon and Dominion conflicts that followed.

The design's longevity produced one final controversy. In 2372 the USS Lakota, an Excelsior refitted with modern weapons well beyond her class's book ratings, fought a brief, bitter engagement against the USS Defiant during an attempted coup inside Starfleet — proof both of the old frame's capacity to absorb upgrades and of how much the Federation had changed around it. By the century's end the class was finally passing out of front-line service, having escorted the fleet from the age of Kirk to the age of the Dominion War; records differ on exact retirement dates, and a handful of hulls served past them regardless.

guides.title: The Intrepid Class
guides.summary: The Intrepid class is Starfleet's fast light explorer of the 2370s — the starship class of USS Voyager — known for its variable-geometry warp nacelles, bio-neural gel pack circuitry, planetary landing capability, and a sustainable cruise speed unmatched by ships many times its size.

sections.heading: Role and Design Intent
sections.body:
The Intrepid class entered Starfleet service in the early 2370s as a light explorer: a fast, science-heavy cruiser intended to carry front-line research capability into regions where a Galaxy-class ship would be an extravagance. At roughly 340 metres and fifteen decks, with a standard complement of around 140, the class trades the great ships' volume for speed, efficiency, and a sensor fit out of proportion to its size.

The design brief emphasised sustained independence. An Intrepid was expected to operate far from starbases for long stretches, so the class received the newest generation of nearly every core system: a compact, high-output warp core, bio-neural computer circuitry, variable-geometry nacelles, and the ability to land on a planetary surface and lift off again under its own power. The result was, at its commissioning, the fastest vessel in the fleet for its size and one of the most technologically dense ships Starfleet had ever fielded — a testbed that happened also to be a superb explorer.

sections.heading: Variable-Geometry Nacelles and Warp Performance
sections.body:
The class's silhouette is defined by its warp nacelles, which do not sit on fixed pylons. At impulse the nacelles lie flat along the engineering hull; at the jump to warp the pylons rotate them upward into flight position. The arrangement was Starfleet's engineering answer to a hard lesson of the 2360s, when research established that conventional warp fields were cumulatively damaging the fabric of subspace along heavily travelled corridors. The variable geometry optimises the field's shape in flight, allowing efficient high-warp cruising without the damage that had forced speed restrictions on older designs.

The performance figures were, for the time, remarkable. The class is rated for a sustainable cruise velocity of warp 9.975 — a figure earlier cruisers could touch only briefly, if at all. In practice the rating made the Intrepid class the natural choice for missions where reach and response time mattered more than mass: patrol in rough border territory, rapid scientific response, and long-range survey work far from support.

sections.heading: Bio-Neural Circuitry
sections.body:
The Intrepid class was among the first to replace much of the traditional isolinear computer network with bio-neural gel packs: sealed units containing cultured synthetic neural fibres suspended in a nutrient medium. The fibres process information the way a brain does, routing around congestion and learning traffic patterns, and the packs give the ship's computer measurably faster response under complex load than isolinear switching alone can manage.

The choice carried a novel cost. Because the gel packs are partly organic, they can sicken. Service records include at least one case of a shipwide infection — traced, in the most famous instance, to microorganisms spread from an ill-advised culinary experiment — that had to be treated medically, with the ship's doctor prescribing for the vessel as for a patient. Engineering crews learned to think of the computer core as something between a machine and a crew member, and the care and replacement of the packs became a standing item of maintenance unlike anything on older classes.

sections.heading: Planetary Landing Capability
sections.body:
Unusually for a starship of its tonnage, an Intrepid can land. The class carries extensible landing struts, inertial and structural systems rated for atmospheric descent, and procedures — the blue-alert protocol — governing the transition from spaceframe to grounded structure. Once down, the ship can conduct repairs, take on raw materials, or shelter from conditions in space that its shields could not outlast, then return to orbit under its own power.

Landing a vessel of some seven hundred thousand metric tonnes is not a casual manoeuvre. The flight rules treat it as a major evolution: the crew secures stations as for combat, the nacelles and field systems reconfigure, and the approach is flown on a precise descent profile with little tolerance for error. Records of the class in service show the capability used sparingly but decisively — most notably by USS Voyager, which set down on several worlds during its Delta Quadrant transit when orbit was impossible or the mission demanded it. No earlier front-line Starfleet cruiser had the option at all.

sections.heading: USS Voyager and the Class in Service
sections.body:
The prototype USS Intrepid proved the design, but the class's history was written by another hull: USS Voyager, launched in 2371 and thrown seventy thousand light-years across the galaxy on its first mission. Voyager's seven-year passage home was an involuntary endurance trial no design board could have staged, and the class passed it — the ship crossed the Delta Quadrant without starbase support, fought engagements its designers never modelled, landed, was rebuilt repeatedly in flight, and came home structurally sound.

Other hulls served closer to home; the USS Bellerophon carried Federation delegations during the Dominion War era, and Intrepid-class ships appear throughout fleet records of the period as scouts, couriers, and survey vessels. But Voyager's journey remains the class's definition in the public mind, and fairly so: nearly every advanced system the design gambled on — the gel packs, the nacelles, the landing gear, the holographic doctor — was proven under conditions harsher than any specification, which is the only proof that finally matters.

guides.title: The Miranda Class
guides.summary: Starfleet's long-serving general-purpose light cruiser of the late twenty-third and twenty-fourth centuries. Covers the Miranda-class starship and its variant starships: the design, the rollbar weapons pod, notable ships such as the USS Reliant, and a service record spanning a century.

sections.heading: Design and Configuration
sections.body:
The Miranda class is organized around a single broad primary hull, with no separate engineering section of the kind carried by many contemporaries. The saucer houses the bridge at its dorsal apex, crew quarters and laboratories through its middle decks, and main engineering, the warp core, and the shuttlebay in its aft third. Two warp nacelles hang on short pylons beneath the hull, keeping the ship's profile low and its mass concentrated.

The class's most recognizable feature is the dorsal rollbar, a reinforced span arching over the saucer that carries a detachable pod. In the standard fit the pod mounts twin torpedo launchers firing forward and aft along with supplementary phaser emitters, giving a compact ship an unusually complete field of fire. Not every hull carries the rollbar; survey and transport variants omit it entirely, and others exchange the weapons pod for sensor arrays or cargo modules. That modularity is deliberate. The spaceframe was drawn from the same component families as the refit heavy cruisers of its era, so shipyards could assemble, repair, and reconfigure Mirandas quickly using parts already in wide circulation.

sections.heading: Entering Service in the Late Twenty-Third Century
sections.body:
The class entered Starfleet service in the 2270s, during the same modernization program that produced the refitted heavy cruisers of the era. Where those ships were fitted out as front-line explorers, the Miranda was conceived as the fleet's general-purpose hull: small enough to build in quantity, large enough to carry a meaningful scientific and tactical load, and simple enough to keep running far from major starbases. It carried the linear warp drive, upgraded phaser banks, and photon torpedo systems standard to its generation, with a crew complement typically in the low hundreds.

Production continued for decades across multiple shipyards, which is one reason registry numbers for the class span such a wide range. By the turn of the twenty-fourth century the Miranda was among the most numerous starship classes in Federation service, and hulls laid down in the first production runs were still being refitted and recommissioned generations later. Few designs in Starfleet history have been carried forward so long with so little change to the basic spaceframe, and none carried forward in such numbers.

sections.heading: Mission Profiles and Variants
sections.body:
Miranda-class ships have served in nearly every role Starfleet assigns. In their first decades they worked as science and survey vessels, and the class became closely associated with long-duration research support; the USS Reliant was on extended survey duty for the Genesis research program when it was lost. Others served as patrol cruisers along contested borders, as convoy escorts, as cargo and personnel transports, and as training ships. The detachable dorsal pod made much of this flexibility possible: weapons, sensors, cargo capacity, or laboratory space could be exchanged at a shipyard without touching the core hull.

Several sub-variants are recorded. Some hulls fly without the rollbar altogether, presenting a clean saucer silhouette. Others carry enlarged outboard housings, and registries describe the Soyuz class, with its extended aft sensor and weapons outriggers, as a close relative built on the same lineage. Later refits replaced computers, shields, and warp systems wholesale while leaving the frame intact, so two Mirandas commissioned a century apart may share little beyond their bones.

sections.heading: Notable Ships and Engagements
sections.body:
The most widely known ship of the class is the USS Reliant, NCC-1864, commandeered in 2285 by the augment Khan Noonien Singh during the Genesis crisis and destroyed in the Mutara Nebula. The USS Saratoga was among the thirty-nine Starfleet vessels lost at Wolf 359 in 2367, when a single Borg cube shattered the fleet assembled to defend Earth.

In the Dominion War of the mid-2370s, Mirandas served in nearly every major fleet action, filling out formations alongside newer classes, screening capital ships, escorting convoys through contested space, and absorbing losses the fleet's records do not disguise: against Jem'Hadar attack ships and Cardassian wings, a century-old light cruiser was often the first hull to fall. They flew in Operation Return, in the assaults on the Chin'toka system, and in the final advance on Cardassia Prime. That so many were available to fight at all, so late in their service lives, is itself the measure of the design.

sections.heading: Why the Class Endured
sections.body:
The Miranda's longevity was not sentiment; it was arithmetic. The spaceframe was cheap to produce, tolerant of refit, and compatible with parts stocked at every major starbase, so keeping an old Miranda flying cost a fraction of building a new hull of equivalent capacity. Its compact single-hull layout made battle damage easier to isolate and repair than on ships with exposed necks and separated engineering sections, and the modular pod meant a hull could change careers in weeks.

Starfleet's posture always needed numbers as much as it needed flagships. For every deep-space explorer, the fleet required dozens of ships to patrol borders, haul freight, chart systems, and show the flag in quiet sectors, and the Miranda filled that need for a hundred years. By the 2370s the class was plainly outmatched ship-for-ship by contemporary threats, and the war spent the surviving hulls hard. But its record, from the Genesis crisis to Wolf 359 to the fall of Cardassia, traces the working history of Starfleet itself, written not by the famous explorers but by the fleet's everyday ships.

guides.title: The Romulan Warbird
guides.summary: The Romulan warbird, chiefly the immense D'deridex class: the Star Empire's cloaked mainline warship of the twenty-fourth century. Covers these warbirds and starships from the artificial singularity core to the Dominion War and the later Valdore-pattern vessels.

sections.heading: The D'deridex at a Glance
sections.body:
The warbird most often meant by the name is the D'deridex class, the mainline heavy warship of the Romulan Star Empire through the middle decades of the twenty-fourth century. It is among the largest vessels fielded by any Alpha or Beta Quadrant power, roughly twice the length of a Federation Galaxy-class explorer, though considerably less dense. The hull is built as an open shell: a raised head section at the bow, shaped in the old Romulan bird-of-prey manner, connects through a long spine to paired dorsal and ventral hulls that sweep back and rejoin at the stern, enclosing a great empty space between them like the gap in a drawn bow.

The plating carries the Empire's characteristic green finish, and the feathered patterning of the surfaces makes the avian intent unmistakable. Internally the class carries a large crew, extensive troop and cargo capacity, and command facilities suited to a vessel that often serves as the senior ship of a formation. It is a ship built to be seen, when the Empire chooses to let it be seen at all.

sections.heading: Power from a Captive Singularity
sections.body:
Where Starfleet vessels generate power by annihilating matter and antimatter, the D'deridex draws its power from an artificial quantum singularity: a forced microscopic black hole held in a containment core, feeding the ship as matter spirals in. The choice reflects Romulan priorities. A singularity core needs no antimatter supply chain, an advantage for a fleet that operates in secrecy far from its own bases, and its emissions differ from those of a warp core, complicating an enemy's attempts to detect or identify the ship.

The cost is inflexibility. Records agree that once initiated, the singularity cannot simply be shut down, and a failing containment system cannot be ejected the way a warp core can. Engagement and boarding reports describe Romulan engineering crews as trained to defend and stabilize the core above almost any other priority. The drive has other quirks, and captured accounts describe strange temporal side effects from badly damaged cores, but in service the design proved reliable enough to power the Empire's front line for decades without evident replacement.

sections.heading: The Cloak and the Doctrine Behind It
sections.body:
The warbird is inseparable from its cloaking device. Romulan doctrine treats space combat as an extension of intelligence work: the preferred engagement is one the enemy never knows is possible until it has already been decided. A D'deridex on patrol is assumed to be cloaked; decloaking is itself a message, staged for effect at a range and bearing of the commander's choosing. Under cloak the ship shadows convoys, maps defenses, and positions itself for the opening salvo, and much of what other powers know about warbird deployments comes from inference rather than observation.

The device is not without limits. Cloaked ships cannot raise shields or fire without dropping the field, minor emissions can betray a careless crew to a patient observer, and specific countermeasures, tachyon detection grids among them, have forced the Empire to keep refining the technology. But the doctrine has never changed. The warbird's size, its disruptor and torpedo armament, and its long endurance all serve the same idea: arrive unseen, reveal yourself only in strength, and let the enemy's imagination do the rest of the work.

sections.heading: Silence, Return, and Standoff
sections.body:
After the Tomed Incident of 2311, the Romulan Star Empire withdrew behind its borders, and for more than half a century the Federation had no confirmed contact. That silence ended in 2364, when a D'deridex-class warbird decloaked before a Federation starship along the Neutral Zone; for many Starfleet officers it was the first Romulan vessel they had ever seen.

The years that followed were a long cold contest conducted almost entirely by warbirds: probing flights along the Zone, surveillance of the Klingon civil war, rescues and defections handled at disruptor range, and repeated standoffs in which fleets faced each other cloaked and uncloaked without a shot fired. Records of these encounters show the class serving as the Empire's instrument of statecraft as much as war, carrying senators, staging deceptions, and enforcing the Empire's insistence on being taken seriously. Through it all the Federation never assembled a complete technical picture of the ship, and assessments of its true capabilities still differ between intelligence services.

sections.heading: The Dominion War and the Later Warbirds
sections.body:
The Empire held aloof from the early Dominion War behind a nonaggression pact, until events in 2374 brought it into open alliance with the Federation and the Klingon Empire. Warbird fleets then appeared in numbers the other powers had only estimated: on the defense lines around the core systems, in the invasion of the Chin'toka system, and in the final assault on Cardassia in 2375. The class fought well but not invulnerably; Dominion weapons killed warbirds as they killed everything else, and the war spent Romulan hulls and Romulan secrecy alike.

By the end of the decade newer types shared the line, lighter and faster warbirds of the Valdore pattern among them, and the events surrounding the Reman-built Scimitar in 2379 showed the Empire's shipbuilding still capable of surprises. Yet the D'deridex remained the shape the word warbird calls to mind: the green double hull hanging silent off a border station, present, unprovable, and entirely intentional.

guides.title: The Sovereign Class
guides.summary: The Sovereign class is the Federation flagship starship class of the late 24th century — the class of the USS Enterprise-E — a heavily armed deep-space explorer shaped by the Borg threat, carrying quantum torpedoes on a frame that still gives half its volume to science and diplomacy.

sections.heading: Origins of the Design
